overview.title: 📖 Overview: Song, and the Date of Destruction
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 12a–12b
overview.hebrewSource: כְּשֶׁחָרַב הַבַּיִת בָּרִאשׁוֹנָה, אוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם תִּשְׁעָה בְּאָב הָיָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Continuing yesterday's question about the Levites' song, the Gemara asks whether wine libations poured on the altar without an accompanying animal offering require song, testing the question against the mournful verse the Levites sang as the Temple fell — ultimately rejected as no real proof, since that verse wasn't even the psalm assigned to that day. The Gemara then works through the baraita's precise dating of the First Temple's destruction — the ninth of Av, a Sunday, the year after a Sabbatical year, during the priestly watch of Yehoyariv — anchoring the calculation to a dated prophecy of Ezekiel and to disputed counts of Nebuchadnezzar's exiles. It tests whether the same 'year after Shmita' holds for the Second Temple's destruction 420 years later, a calculation that only works under Rabbi Yehuda's view of how Jubilee years are counted, before an alternative answer notes that the priestly watch of Yehoyariv could not literally have existed by the time of the Second Temple at all.

slides.title: 🍷 Do Standalone Wine Libations Require Song?
slides.subtitle: A dilemma left over from yesterday's discussion

nodes.content: ❓ Wine libations poured on the altar WITHOUT an accompanying animal offering — do they require the Levites' song?
💭 Attempted proof: as the Temple fell, the Levites sang — yet no obligatory OR voluntary burnt offering was being sacrificed that day. Perhaps it was sung for libations alone?

columns.label: Rava/Rav Ashi reject this
columns.content: The verse they sang belongs to Wednesday's psalm, not Sunday's — a spontaneous lament, not an actual accompanying song

columns.label: Reish Lakish's fallback
columns.content: Levites may sing on the platform with NO offering at all — so 'standing on their platform' proves nothing either way

nodes.content: ⚠️ If song is optional without any offering, why not allow it for libations too? Answer: doing so risks people assuming song is optional even for a full offering — the question remains open

slides.title: 📅 Dating the First Temple's Destruction
slides.subtitle: Four converging details, all anchored to a dated prophecy of Ezekiel
rows: The year after a Sabbatical year

callout.label: The anchor verse:
callout.text: Ezekiel 40:1 dates a prophecy '25 years into the exile...at the beginning of the year, on the tenth of the month, 14 years after the city was struck' — read as pinpointing a Jubilee year, since a Jubilee begins on the tenth of Tishrei, Yom Kippur.

slides.title: 🔢 420 Years — Did the Second Temple Fall the Same Way?
slides.subtitle: Testing whether the Second Temple's destruction also lands in the year after Shmita

steps.content: 1️⃣ The Second Temple stood 420 years; the Gemara checks whether this also lands in the year after a Sabbatical year
2️⃣ A straightforward count (8 Jubilees of 50 years = 400, plus 2 more Shmita cycles = 14, plus 6 remaining) puts the destruction IN a Shmita year, not after it

3️⃣ Under Rabbi Yehuda's view — that a Jubilee year doubles as year one of the NEXT cycle, so each cycle is only 49 years — the extra years shift the total to land in the year AFTER Shmita, matching the baraita

4️⃣ But applying that same math to the FIRST Temple throws its date off — resolved only by excluding the years of the Ten Tribes' exile under Sennacherib from the Jubilee count, since a Jubilee requires all twelve tribes in their land

slides.title: 🎭 Or Maybe the Details Simply Don't All Match
slides.subtitle: A simpler alternative resolution
slides.label: A simpler answer:
slides.text: Perhaps the baraita's phrase 'and likewise for the second [Temple]' never claimed an identical Shmita-year timing — only the same day of the week and month, the 9th of Av on a Sunday. This must be the more limited reading regardless, since the baraita's detail that the priestly watch of Yehoyariv was on duty literally cannot apply to the Second Temple: only four families of priests returned from the Babylonian exile, and Yehoyariv's original watch, from before the exile, no longer existed by then.

slides.title: ⛓️ Rebuilding the 24 Priestly Watches After the Exile
slides.subtitle: How four returning families became twenty-four again

steps.content: 1️⃣ Only four of the original twenty-four priestly families returned from Babylonia: Yedaya, Ḥarim, Pashḥur, and Immer
2️⃣ The prophets among the returnees divided these four families into twenty-four new watches, to restore the original structure
3️⃣ Slips bearing the twenty-four new watch-names were mixed together and placed in a lottery receptacle (קַלְפִּי)
4️⃣ Yedaya's representative drew first, receiving his own watch's portion plus five more — six watches in total for his family, and so on for the others

summary.principle: The Gemara pursues the precise scope of the Levites' song with the same exactness it brings to dating the Temple's destruction: an apparent proof from history collapses once the details are checked against the actual weekly psalm-cycle and the actual composition of the priesthood after the exile.

flowSteps.content: 🍷 Do standalone libations require song? A proof from the Temple's destruction fails — that verse wasn't even the day's assigned psalm
📅 First Temple's destruction dated via Ezekiel's prophecy: 9 Av, a Sunday, year after Shmita, watch of Yehoyariv

columns.content: 🔢 The Second Temple's 420-year span matches only under Rabbi Yehuda's Jubilee-counting method
🎭 Yehoyariv's watch didn't even exist by the Second Temple — only 4 families returned, later divided into 24 by lottery

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: aggadic claims about the Temple's destruction are checked against verifiable calendrical and historical detail, not accepted at face value

quiz.q: What is the Gemara's dilemma regarding wine libations poured on the altar?
o: Whether they may be poured by a non-priest
Whether the Levites must sing when only libations, without an accompanying animal offering, are brought
Whether libations require salt
Whether libations may be brought on Shabbat
quiz.e: The dilemma is specifically whether standalone libations (nesachim habaim bifnei atzman) require the Levites' song, parallel to the earlier question about voluntary burnt offerings.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara reject the idea that the Levites' verse as the Temple fell proves anything about which offerings require song?
o: Because the Levites were forbidden to sing that day
That verse belongs to the psalm assigned to Wednesday, not Sunday (the actual day of destruction), showing it was a spontaneous lament rather than an actual accompanying song
Because no Levites were present at the destruction
Because the verse was sung in the wrong location
quiz.e: Rava (or Rav Ashi) points out the mismatch between the weekly psalm cycle and the verse actually sung, showing it cannot serve as proof about the halakha of song accompanying offerings.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's reading of Ezekiel 40:1, what detail helps pin down that the First Temple's destruction fell in the year after a Sabbatical year?
o: The verse's mention of 'the tenth of the month' at 'the beginning of the year,' which matches a Jubilee year beginning on the tenth of Tishrei (Yom Kippur)
The verse's mention of a solar eclipse
A direct statement in the verse naming the Sabbatical year
The verse's reference to the priestly watch of Yehoyariv
quiz.e: The Gemara reads Ezekiel's dating of his prophecy as identifying a Jubilee year specifically, since a Jubilee year begins on the tenth of Tishrei, matching the verse's 'beginning of the year, on the tenth of the month.'

quiz.q: Under whose opinion does the calculation work out that the Second Temple, which stood 420 years, was also destroyed in the year after a Sabbatical year?
o: Rabbi Meir's opinion that all counting is symbolic
Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that the Jubilee (fiftieth) year counts as both the last year of one cycle and the first year of the next
Rabbi Yosei's opinion that the Jubilee is exactly fifty years with no overlap
There is no opinion under which the calculation works
quiz.e: Only Rabbi Yehuda's view, which effectively shortens each cycle to forty-nine years by double-counting the Jubilee year, produces the extra years needed to match the baraita's claim.

quiz.q: Why couldn't the priestly watch of Yehoyariv literally have been on duty when the Second Temple was destroyed?
o: Because priests were forbidden from serving during the Second Temple period
Because only four priestly families returned from the Babylonian exile, and they were later divided by lottery into new watches of twenty-four — Yehoyariv's original watch no longer existed
Because the Second Temple had no priestly watches at all
Because Yehoyariv's family had converted to another religion
quiz.e: The Gemara notes that only four families (Yedaya, Ḥarim, Pashḥur, and Immer) returned from exile and were reorganized by lottery into twenty-four new watches, so the original watch of Yehoyariv from before the exile was gone.
